L1@P0: Canine Autologous
L2@P0: Nanoparticle Cancer
L3@P0: Vaccine (V4)
L4@P0: Immunotherapy For Dogs
L5@P0: Dr Chris Weir
L6@P0: Principal Scientist | Dog Oncology Group Pty Ltd.
L7@P0: e. dr.c.w@outlook.com
L8@P0: C&T No. 6027
L9@P0: Some cancers produce unique proteins or antigens on
L10@P0: their surface which differ from that of a normal cell.
L11@P0: These proteins can provide a target for the immune
L12@P0: system. CANCV-4 utilises the dog’s own cancer tissue to
L13@P0: produce a vaccine which ‘re-educates’ and stimulates
L14@P0: the immune system so it recognises and targets the
L15@P0: cancer.
L16@P0: The Evolution: CACV-1—CANCV-4
L17@P0: Over a period of 7 years CANCV has been tested, refined,
L18@P0: and improved to increase levels of immune stimulation
L19@P0: and response:
L20@P0: CACV-1 Used a commercially available adjuvant—
L21@P0: immunity waned over time and no
L22@P0: apparent response in tumour types like
L23@P0: Melanoma. Results of this initial cohort
L24@P0: were published Vet. Sci. 2018, 5(4), 87;
L25@P0: doi.org/10.3390/vetsci5040087
L26@P0: CANCV-2 Nanoparticle adjuvant was introduced
L27@P0: to replace commercially available one
L28@P0: after increased efficacy was seen in
L29@P0: rodent cancer models.
L30@P0: CANCV-3 Higher dose nanoparticles and
L31@P0: improved cancer protein isolation and
L32@P0: extraction. Introduction of immune
L33@P0: stimulant into the vaccine to draw more
L34@P0: immune cells into the vaccination site.
L35@P0: CANCV-4 Further modified nanoparticles for
L36@P0: increased immune stimulation with
L37@P0: improved dendritic cell uptake and
L38@P0: antigen presentation to T cells.
L39@P0: Incorporation of tumour antigens into or
L40@P0: onto the nanoparticle for slower release
L41@P0: and improved immune cell uptake.
L42@P0: Ability to use fresh, frozen, formalin
L43@P0: fixed or paraffin embedded tumour
L44@P0: tissue.
L45@P0: The Process
L46@P0: Fresh or frozen tissue is collected and sent to the lab for
L47@P0: processing. Formalin fixed, paraffin embedded tissue
L48@P0: can also be used to make a vaccine, but this takes longer
L49@P0: to process (4 days). The process involves:
L50@P0: 1. Processing the tissue to a singular protein level.
L51@P0: 2. Treating the proteins to expose
L52@P0: more potential antigens.
L53@P0: 3. Combining with or incorporating the antigens
L54@P0: into the nanoparticles with immune stimulant.
L55@P0: 4. Bottling for administration.
L56@P0: CANCV-4 DOSING SCHEDULE
L57@P0: Initial doses (0.4 mL) are given intramuscularly 4 x weekly,
L58@P0: 2 x weekly and 2 x fortnightly or 4 x fortnightly and then
L59@P0: four monthly boosters are administered. Depending on
L60@P0: your dog’s cancer scenario and sample size, more doses
L61@P0: can be made and administered after initial course.
L62@P0: Safety
L63@P0: Various versions of CANCV have been used to treat over
L64@P0: 700 dogs with different types of cancer. Minor, temporary
L65@P0: side-effects, lasting 24-48 hours may occur, such as
L66@P0: lumps at the vaccination site, malaise, fatigue, or loss of
L67@P0: appetite. No major side effects or anaphylaxis seen.
L68@P0: Scenarios for Use
L69@P0: Primary treatment—following tumour removal by surgery

L8: #### Our Mission
L9: 
L10: * * *
L11: 
L12: 【2†Image†img1.wsimg.com】
L13: 
L14: #### To improve the lives of dogs, cats and horses with cancer by providing safe, personalized immunotherapy that harnesses each patient's own immune system to fight cancer and extend survival.
L15: #### About us
L16: 
L17: D.O.G founder and lead research scientist, Dr Chris Weir, has been creating personalised vaccines for animals for over 16 years. The CANCV vaccine is the result of over a decade of testing and refinement to optimise the immune response to the cancer. CANCV is available through experienced oncologists and veterinarians.
L18: 
L19: 【3†Enquiries】
L20: #### Overview of Immunotherapy for dogs, cats and horses
L21: 
L22: Canine Autologous Nanoparticle Cancer Vaccine (CANCV)
L23: CANCV is a cutting-edge vaccine developed for canine cancer treatment, utilising the dog’s own cancer tissue to create a personalised vaccine that stimulates the immune system to recognise and target the cancer cells. Many cancers in dogs produce unique antigens or proteins on their surface that differ from normal cells.
L24: CANCV takes advantage of these distinct markers to enhance the immune system's ability to detect and attack cancerous cells, effectively providing a tailored immunotherapy approach for dogs, cats and horses suffering from various types of cancer.
L25: #### CANCV - Process and Patients
L26: 
L27: * * *
L28: #### Process of Creating the Vaccine (CANCV)
L29: The vaccine production begins by collecting fresh, frozen, formalin-fixed or paraffin embedded tissue from the dog. The tissue is processed to isolate tumour proteins, which are then treated to expose tumour antigens (TA). These TAs are combined with calcium-based nanoparticles and immune stimulants to create the vaccine, which is subsequently bottled for administration. A typical vaccine course requires approximately 0.2g of tumour tissue for an initial eight-dose regimen.
L30: Once sample arrives at the laboratory the vaccine can take 1-3 days to make depending on the sample type.
L31: #### Dosing Schedule
L32: 
L33: The typical dosing schedule for CANCV begins with four initial doses given intramuscularly (I.M) weekly for 4 weeks (0.4 mL each dose). Subsequent doses are typically given monthly for a total of 8 dose. Your Oncologist or vet may recommend an alternative schedule based on the type and stage of cancer or to work alongside chemotherapy or radiotherapy protocols.

L3: # Perth dogs helping to fight cancer
L4:

L6: 
L7: 【5†Image: a dog being treated in a medical facility】
L8: 
L9: Immunotherapy is the new holy grail of cancer treatment – using the patient’s own immune system to fight the disease.
L10: But this revolutionary therapy has had little impact on solid tumours like sarcoma, the third most common cancer in children. Now, a world-first trial at The Kids Research Institute Australia could change that – all with the help of man’s best friend.
L11: 
L12: The busy pre-surgery area of Perth Veterinary Specialists in Osborne Park is perhaps the last place you’d expect to be ground zero for a clinical trial that could save the lives of thousands of kids around the world.
L13: This is where three-year-old bulldog, Maggie, is waiting to go under the knife to remove a small but potentially deadly sarcoma tumour on her back and earn herself a place in medical research history.
L14: Maggie is one of a handful of dogs selected to trial a cutting-edge new treatment for sarcoma. A polymer-filled gel, loaded with immunotherapy drugs, will be applied inside the wound when the skilled vet surgeon removes her tumour. She’ll then be stitched up and sent home, while the gel kicks her canine immune system into action.
L15: 
L16: This clinical trial in Perth dogs is the brainchild of 【6†Associate Professor Joost Lesterhuis】, Head of the 【7†The Kids Cancer Centre†cancer.thekids.org.au】.
L17: “Surprisingly, sarcoma in dogs presents similarly to sarcoma in humans. The treatment is much the same – surgery to remove the tumour. In kids, this is followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy,” Associate Professor Lesterhuis said.
L18: 
L19: “But it’s not a perfect treatment. The cancer can come back in the same spot. Invisible cancer cells make their way into the surrounding tissue, so it’s impossible for a surgeon to know if they’ve got all the cancer.”
L20: The immunotherapy gel is designed to mop up those remaining cancer cells by activating the body’s own immune system and drawing immune cells to the site of the cancer.
L21: 
L22: Associate Professor Lesterhuis said the gel, developed with the help of chemists at The University of Western Australia, could revolutionise the way solid tumours were treated.

L40: # Dogs with cancer could leave lasting legacy
L41: 
L42: 6 February 2026
L43: 
L44: 【23†Image: A female and male academic kneel down with a cavoodle on the grass】
L45: 
L46: Professor Rachel Allavena and Dr José Granados Soler urge owners of eligible dogs to apply for the trial.
L47: 
L48: (Photo credit: The University of Queensland )
L49: 
L50: A University of Queensland project could be a glimmer of hope for dogs suffering from inoperable or incurable cancers.
L51: The project will test the effectiveness of immunomodulatory drug Enzistat in treating solid tumours caused by naturally occurring cancers, including soft tissue sarcoma, mast cell tumour and melanoma.
L52: 
L53: 【24†Professor Rachel Allavena†veterinary-science.uq.edu.au】 from UQ’s 【25†School of Veterinary Science†veterinary-science.uq.edu.au】 said owners who had been told their dog’s cancer was terminal or their pet’s tumours were inoperable should apply for the trial.
L54: “The 6-week treatment consists of oral tablet Enzistat being administered twice daily, regular consultations, blood samples and biopsies,” Professor Allavena said.
L55: 
L56: “Enzistat is designed to target advanced cancers by activating the patient’s immune system.
L57: 
L58: > “Previous compassionate use trials showed Enzistat achieved tumour regression and increased survival time for palliative patients with advanced, late-stage cancers, supporting further evaluation in a formal trial.
L59: “The research consists of 2 trials with the first focusing on terminal patients where the aim is to prolong their lives.
L60: 
L61: “The second aims to see if the drug can shrink large tumours to allow for surgical removal.”
L62: 
L63: To be eligible for participation, dogs must have received a cancer diagnosis from their vet and be able to provide medical records.
L64: 
L65: Researchers will work with the dogs' regular vet throughout the duration of the trial.
